paragraph: Disregarding Dasaratha's piteous impassioned pleas, Parasurama said to Rama "There existed in this world two bows, you destroyed one and the other is the one given by the devatas to lord Visnu. Goaded by the devatas who wanted to test the strength of Siva and Visnu. Brahma instigated a quarrel between the two gods. In that conflict the bow of Siva was rendered motionless by a single 'Hunkara' 'from Visnu. Witnessing what had ensued, Visnu was deemed the more valiant. In his fury, Maheswara taking the bow gave it to Devarata, the renowned king of Videha. The bow of Visnu was given in trust to Richika son of Bhrigu and passed on to Jamadagni. When Jamadagni renounced his weapons, Kartaviryarjuna foolishly killed him. Furious at my father's death I went on a rampage killing the Kshatriyas again and again, as they were born and reborn! Having conquered the earth, I gave it away to that magnanimous and noble sage Kasyapa. I had since retired to the Mahendra mountain in pursuit of my penance and I am now here having heard of the bow of Siva and its destruction. String this bow of Vishnu now!"
Chapter/Canto/Verse_Reference: Bala Kanda, Sarga 75 (Parasurama Explains the Two Bows and Challenges Rama)
Situation/Problem_Faced: Parasurama ignores Dasaratha's desperate pleas and addresses Rama directly. He reveals the existence of two divine bows (Siva's and Vishnu's), explaining a past conflict orchestrated by Brahma to determine the greater deity, in which Vishnu proved superior. He recounts the lineage of Vishnu's bow, leading to its current possession by him (Parasurama). Driven by his long-standing fury over his father Jamadagni's death by Kartaviryarjuna, he reiterates his past genocidal rampage against Kshatriyas and challenges Rama to string Vishnu's bow, implying a continuation of his mission.
Key_Teaching/Action_Taken: This passage is crucial as it reveals the divine context of Rama and Parasurama's confrontation. It establishes that Parasurama is not just a vengeful Brahmin but a manifestation of Vishnu's power from a previous era, serving to test the new incarnation. The narrative of the two bows and the past conflict between Siva and Vishnu highlights the supremacy of Vishnu's power. Parasurama's continued anger against the Kshatriyas (despite his past actions of renunciation) sets up the ultimate test for Rama: to prove his own supreme Vishnu-like power and calm the lingering wrath of the previous age.
Outcome/Resolution: Parasurama dismisses Dasaratha's pleas and explains to Rama the history of the two divine bows and the past contest between Siva and Vishnu, where Vishnu proved superior. He then details how Vishnu's bow came into his possession. Driven by his unresolved anger over his father's death, Parasurama challenges Rama to string Vishnu's bow, setting the stage for a climactic showdown that will determine the supreme divine power.

Spiritual_Psychological_Concept_Indian.Concept: Avatara (Incarnation - testing of one Avatara by another)
Tejas (Radiance/Spiritual Power - the power of Vishnu's bow and its wielder)
Lila (Divine Play - the encounter as a cosmic unfolding)

Brief_Summary_Spiritual: Parasurama, disregarding Dasaratha's pleas, reveals the divine 'Lila' (play) behind the two bows and the past testing of Siva and Vishnu's 'Tejas' (spiritual power), establishing Vishnu's supremacy. His challenge to Rama to string Vishnu's bow is a direct confrontation between two 'Avataras' (incarnations) of Vishnu, driven by Parasurama's lingering 'Krodha' (anger) and 'Sankalpa' (resolve) to eliminate Kshatriyas. This encounter is crucial for the transfer of divine power and the confirmation of Rama's ultimate spiritual authority.
Brief_Summary_Psychological: Psychologically, Parasurama's monologue reveals a character deeply consumed by unresolved anger and a formidable ego. His disregard for Dasaratha's emotional plea shows a lack of empathy, entirely focused on his personal mission. By narrating the history of the bows and the past divine test, he sets a psychological stage for a direct challenge to Rama's self-esteem and perceived power. This confrontation is framed as a test of supremacy, driven by Parasurama's psychological need to affirm his own formidable identity and legacy against a rising new power.
